First, I check whether a schema or parser for `Order` already exists, so I don't hand-roll a parallel type: `Grep "OrderSchema|parseOrder|z.object" --type ts`.
I follow "External data is untyped until parsed" and "Don't lie to the type system". The `as Order` cast is a latent crash: `order.items.length` throws if the body has no `items`.
I replace the cast with a parse at the boundary: `const order = OrderSchema.parse(JSON.parse(body));`, returning 400 on a ZodError.
If no schema exists, I define `OrderSchema` with zod and derive the type from it: `type Order = z.infer<typeof OrderSchema>`. If an authoritative spec like OpenAPI exists, I generate the type from that spec instead.
After that, the downstream `order.items.length` can trust the type.

### Intent
> The user found the jbus view UI subpar: no header, no sidebar, no navigation. This PR adds a header (name, where you are, time of the last read) and a sidebar ("All", then each project with its waits count and a health dot, turning into chips under 900 px). It draws Room, jbus and Runners once as the machine's and never inside a project. It fixes the Bus card wrapping and sideways scroll at 1440/900/390, and folds empty lanes. All of it stays vanilla JS/CSS in the one page and its panels, inside the user's word caps (250 overview, 150 project). `make check` and `jgauge test-slot -- make check` must pass.

### Reviewers
- Reviewer A: 8 findings
- Reviewer B: 9 findings
- Both reviewers found the same four things independently: the word-cap change, the duplicated health rules, the file length, and the missing machine row on the no-project view. Each also found real bugs the other missed. All of the review skill's questions were asked.

### Act On

**1. The header shows the current time as "read" while the server is unreachable** (A3)
After `MISS` failed polls, `lost()` sets `NOW = Date.now()` and re-renders. The header at `src/jbus/view/page.html:752` then says "read <now>", and the time moves forward on every failed poll. "The time of the last read" is a Done-when line, and this is the one moment it matters. The PR changed the label, so the wrong value is now presented as a fact.
- **Fix:** keep the time of the last successful answer as its own value (set it in `took`/`tookStack`) and show that.

**2. The word caps are met by moving content out of what is counted** (A4, B1, B2)
`probe.js:103-104` now counts only `<main>`. The machine row, header and sidebar go into a separate `SHELL = 30` budget (`tests/test_jbus_view_page.py:100`). The user's caps were for what the first screen shows. The new content was not made to fit; it was moved outside the measurement, which makes the test a proxy.

`SHELL = 30` is also a fixed number, while the docstring says the shell grows with each project. The three-project fixture is at about 26 words, so two more projects fail the test with nothing wrong on the page.
- **Fix:** count the whole first screen against `WORDS`/`EVERY`. If the shell genuinely needs room, that is a gate for `jbus gate`, not a quiet relaxation. Any shell-only figure should scale with project count, and be tested with more than three projects.

**3. The health rules exist twice, and the copies already disagree** (A2, B5)
`troubles()` at `page.html:670-678` re-implements the amber rules that the row chips already apply (`page.html:716-723`). Concrete differences today:
- `troubles` ignores `h.blind`, so a project with blind spots gets an amber "Blind 6" chip but a green sidebar dot.
- It treats `threads == null` differently from the row.
- Line 673 prints "0 failed wakes, last error: X" when only `last_error` is set, a case the row chip guards against.

The dot is the sidebar's main signal, so this is a correctness issue.
- **Fix:** one per-fact helper returning `[state, text, tip]` entries. The row draws the entries as chips; the dot is amber if any entry is `op`.

**4. The sidebar stays empty for up to 15 s on a link to a missing project** (A1)
The path is concrete:
1. The 404 from `/state.json` arrives first and sets `S = null`, then renders with `STACK` still null.
2. When `/stack.json` arrives, the render sits behind `if (S)`, so nothing is redrawn.
3. The sidebar stays empty until the next poll.

The "no such project" page is something the user specifically asked for.
- **Fix:** drop the `S` guard (`put` already skips unchanged parts), and add a test that loads `#/nope` and checks the sidebar items after the first poll.

**5. The jbus item on a project page can show a false "passing"** (B3)
`unwell` comes from `STACK.machine.unwell`, which is refreshed only every fourth poll. If `/stack.json` fails, its error handler does nothing (`page.html:1002`), `STACK` stays null, and `unwell` becomes `[]`. The jbus item then shows ok/"passing" while the rest of the row comes from a fresh read. A false green on a health view is worse than no signal.
- **Minimum fix (inside Where):** don't render ok when there is no stack read.
- **Better fix:** derive `unwell` from the page's own `S.sources`. If that needs a `machine` flag from the server, the server change is outside Where and is noted for later.

**6. A comment now contradicts the poll code** (B7)
`page.html:994` says "One request a poll", but project pages now also ask for `/stack.json`. It is a one-line fix next to the changed lines, and leaving it is how the next person misreads the poll.

### Consider

**The page passes 1,000 lines** (A5, B4)
`page.html` goes from 979 to 1067 lines. The user asked for "one vanilla file", but `panels/` already inlines per-part scripts server-side, so a `shell` script there would still be served as one file. The cost is unknown: if inlining a new script needs a change to `__init__.py`/`state.py`, that is outside Where.
- **Recommendation:** split it if the panel loader picks up new files without code changes; otherwise note it for the next PR.

**The machine row is missing on views with no project read** (A7, B6)
`machineOf` returns null when `PROJECT` is set and `S` is null, which covers the first load and the not-found page. That contradicts the new test docstring ("drawn once, on every view"). The fix is one line (fall back to `STACK.machine` without drawers), and it pairs naturally with Act-on item 4.
- **Tradeoff:** these are edge views, but the fix is cheap. Do it while fixing item 4.

**The theme picker became one cycling button** (A8, B9)
The task did not ask for a new picker, and the cycling is untested. There may be a real reason: three buttons may not fit the header at 390 px.
- **Recommendation:** if space forced it, say so in the PR and add a click test for auto → light → dark → auto and the stored value. If it didn't, restore the three buttons inside the header.

**The sidebar's sticky offset assumes a 50 px header** (A6, B8)
The header wraps (long crumbs, or "asking the server"), so between 900 and 1100 px the sticky sidebar can slide under it. No test checks this, because the browser tests only check sideways scroll.
- **Tradeoff:** it's a nit, but a CSS variable shared by `.hdr` and `.side` costs two lines.

### Noted
- Nothing else. Neither reviewer padded with style preferences; even the nits point to concrete failure paths.

### Dismissed
- None. No finding rested on missing context or a preference for a different approach.

### Agreement Map
The reviewers agreed on the structural issues: the word-cap proxy, the duplicated health rules, file length, the missing machine row on the no-project view, the sticky offset, and the theme redesign. That convergence makes the cap and health-rule findings the strongest signals in the review.

They diverged on runtime ordering and freshness bugs, which each found alone: A found the stale "read" time and the empty sidebar after a 404, and B found the stale/empty `unwell` and the "0 failed wakes" text. These are the findings that need tracing through poll timing, and they are real execution paths, not hypotheticals.

The pattern: the layout work largely meets the Done-when lines. The weak points are where the new shell reads data (`NOW`, `STACK`, `S`) on a different schedule from the panels, and a test change that quietly moved the user's word caps. Fix the data sources and restore the full-screen word count, and this is close to mergeable.

### Intent
> Replace the two pr-review reviewer subagents (A/B) per PR with one review thread. That thread reads the diff itself with the same intent, `SCOPE` and seven questions, and keeps the blast-radius proof. It sends the crewmate one combined review and writes one `## Review` section with every line jmerge and jbus read (`Reviewers: 1`). jmerge's ready rule must still pass, with `ready.py` untouched unless a test proves otherwise. jbus archives, and does not only settle, a review thread when its PR merges or closes, and never archives one whose PR is open. Skills and docs that say "two reviewers" now say one. Tests must cover the skill text, the archive on merge vs. open, and jmerge reading the new section as ready. `make check` exits 0.

### Reviewers
- Reviewer A: 8 findings
- Reviewer B: 4 findings
- The reviewers did not agree on everything, but three findings were raised independently by both: the "closed" inference in `shut()`, the false Step 4 sentence, and the files outside `Where`. Both reviewers answered the review skill's seven questions.

### Act On

**1. `shut()` infers "closed" from absence and then archives, so an open PR's review thread can be archived.** (A2, B1)
- `src/jbus/threads.py:164` treats a slug as closed when its Result's URL string is missing from a 100-item open list.
- That list is incomplete in three ways: a 101st open PR, a URL in a different form, or a PR opened under another slug's branch.
- The Done when line says "a review thread of an open pull request is never archived", and archiving is the one step jbus never undoes.
- B adds that `watch.pull()` already defines MERGED/CLOSED. A second rule that disagrees with it is a correctness bug as well as duplication.
- Fix: derive "ended" from `pull(world, slug, …) in (MERGED, CLOSED)`. If that rule is itself built on absence, confirm the closed state from GitHub before archiving.
- This is the most important item: both reviewers found it, it has a concrete execution path, and the action is destructive.

**2. The "new shape is ready" test never lists a finding.** (A1)
- The template line is `Findings:` with no space after the colon, so the `": "` fill never applies and the listed finding is dropped.
- `ready.py` then sees `found == 0`. The rule that a finding must be answered is never exercised.
- That rule is exactly what the Done when line asks the test to prove.
- Fix: put a real `- warning …` item under `Findings:` and add the negative case, where the same section with no `Finding:` answer is not ready.

**3. `docs/flow.html:214` still says "Two reviewers … then settles itself".** (A3)
- This is a Done when line the PR does not meet: "any other skill or doc that tells pr-review to start two reviewers says one".
- It is a one-line fix. The page is hand-written, not generated, so the docs sweep will not correct it.

**4. Step 4 of the skill claims the judgment has context the reading lacked.** (A6, B2)
- `skills/pr-review/SKILL.md:232` survives from the two-subagent design. In one thread it is false.
- It is worse than stale: it tells the reviewer it has an independent cross-check that no longer exists.
- Skill text is the code here, and the fix is one sentence inside `Where`. Say the reading and the judgment are the same thread, and point the judgment at re-checking each claim against the repo and brief.

### Consider

**5. `finished()` puts an `"archive"` mode key into a map keyed by title prefix.** (A4)
- Computing `ended` once in `settle` and choosing the actions per thread would remove the special case, the `shelve` propagation and the nested loop.
- This is real simplification, not just preference.
- Tradeoff: the fix for item 1 rewrites `shut()`/`ended` anyway, so doing this alongside it is cheap. If it isn't done then, it can wait.

**6. A merged PR whose last Review is `not run` never gets its review threads archived.** (A5)
- After a merge, nothing waits on the thread, and the Done when line says the archive happens "on the next pass".
- Tradeoff: it is an edge case (a later scoped pass that stopped early). The fix is small, but it widens what gets archived.
- At minimum, `docs/jbus.md` should say this is deliberate.

### Noted
- **Files outside `Where`** (A7, B4): `README.md`, `docs/flow.md` and `docs/jgauge.md` are required by the Done when docs line. `src/jbus/t3.py` is required because `_held` refused `archive`. Each change traces to the task; the brief's `Where` was too narrow.

  - The claim about how T3 lists archived threads is unverified.
  - The leftover subagents only exist for reviews started under the old skill, and new reviews have none.
  - Low impact, and it shrinks to nothing over time.

### Dismissed
- None. Every finding was either correct or justified in context; the out-of-scope items were noted rather than rejected.

### Agreement Map
- **Agreed:** both reviewers converged on the riskiest code, `shut()`. A framed it as a broken invariant (an open PR's thread gets archived) and B as a second definition of the same rule. ### Intent
> Replace pr-review's two reviewer subagents (A/B) with one scoped review thread. That thread reads only the PR's diff with the same intent, `SCOPE` and seven questions, keeps the blast-radius proof, and writes one `## Review` section with `Reviewers: 1`. jmerge's `ready.py` must still read that section as ready without changes. jbus must archive, not only settle, a PR's `review:` thread once the PR merges or closes, and must never archive the review thread of an open PR. Every skill or doc that says "two reviewers" must say one. Tests cover the skill text, the archive on merge vs. open, and jmerge readiness of the new shape. `make check` exits 0.

### Reviewers
- Reviewer A: 8 findings
- Reviewer B: 4 findings
- The two agreed on three points: `shut()`'s closed rule, the stale step-4 sentence, and the files outside `Where`. Each also found things the other missed. The review skill's seven questions were asked.

### Act On

**1. `shut()` infers "closed" from absence and then archives (A2, B1)**
`shut()` treats a slug as closed when its Result's `Branch:` URL string is not among the open-PR URLs. That list is capped at 100, and the comparison is raw string matching.
- Any open PR that falls outside the list, or whose URL differs only in form, gets its review thread archived. That breaks the Done-when line "a review thread of an open pull request is never archived".
- The archive is destructive, and jbus never undoes it.
- B adds that `watch.pull()` already defines MERGED/CLOSED, and the new test's `eta` case shows the two rules disagreeing about the same brief.

The fix: use `watch.pull()`, which keeps "merged or closed" defined in one place and avoids a second, weaker rule. If `pull()` also infers CLOSED from absence, archive only on `world.merged` or a GitHub-confirmed `CLOSED` state. Two reviewers found this independently, with a concrete path, against a hard constraint.

**2. The jmerge "new shape" test never lists a finding (A1)**
- The template line is `Findings:` with no `": "`, so the fill step never inserts the finding item, and the `.replace` does nothing.
- jmerge therefore sees `found == 0`, and the "findings answered" half of the ready rule goes untested.
- The test would keep passing if findings/answers matching broke.

The fix: write the `- warning …` item under `Findings:` explicitly, and add the negative case where the same section without its `Finding:` line is not ready. This Done-when test exists to prove the readiness rule, and it doesn't.

**3. `docs/flow.html` still says "Two reviewers … then settles itself" (A3)**
- The Done-when line covers "any other skill or doc", and this page is hand-written, not generated, so it is in scope.
- Nothing in `test_flow_doc.py` catches it.

The fix: correct the text. A cheap grep-style test for "two reviewers" / "reviewer A" across `docs/` and `skills/` would also stop this recurring.

**4. Step 4's "what the reading was not given" is now false (A6, B2)**
`skills/pr-review/SKILL.md:232` tells the lead step it has context the reading lacked. In one thread, the reading read the whole brief. The skill text is the product here, and a false claim of an independent cross-check misleads every future review.

The fix: reword step 4 to say what the judgment actually adds, which is re-checking each claim against the repo and brief, plus the dismissal discipline. It's a one-line fix, and both reviewers flagged it.

### Consider

**5. `finished()` mixes an `"archive"` mode key into a title-prefix map (A4)**
Computing `ended` once in `settle` and deriving `("settle", "archive")` from the review prefix plus the slug would remove the dict key, the `shelve` propagation and the nested loop. That simplification is real.

The tradeoff: it is structural, not a bug. Fixing item 1 will rework this code anyway, so do it as part of that change rather than separately.

**6. A merged PR whose last Review is `not run` never gets its review threads archived (A5)**
The Done-when line says a review thread is archived on merge, and after a merge the thread waits on nothing.

The tradeoff: it needs a later pass that wrote `not run`, which is an uncommon path. Either archive the non-busy review threads of ended slugs regardless of verdict, or document in `docs/jbus.md` that they are kept on purpose. The first is the better match for the intent.

### Noted
- **Files outside `Where`: `README.md`, `docs/flow.md`, `docs/jgauge.md`, `src/jbus/t3.py` (A7, B4).** Every changed line traces to the task. The docs fall under the "any other doc" line, and `t3.py` was required because `_held` refused `archive`. Not harmful; the brief's `Where` was simply too narrow.
- **Ambiguous `docs/jbus.md:108` sentence (A8).** It is a phrasing nit. Worth fixing while touching that file for item 6.
- **Test fake keeps archived threads listed; already-settled legacy A/B subagents are not archived (B3).** How T3 lists archived threads is hypothetical, and the current fake covers the "still listed" case. Settled legacy subagents only affect reviews written before this change, and new PRs have none. This is low impact.

### Dismissed
None. Every finding was grounded. The weakest ones are noted rather than dismissed.

### Agreement Map
Both reviewers converged on the archive rule (items 1 and 4 above, plus the out-of-`Where` files), which is the strongest signal in this review: the destructive path rests on a weak inference. B framed it as duplicated logic, and A framed it as a violated constraint. Both framings lead to the same fix, reusing `watch.pull()`.

That thread reads the PR's diff itself, keeps the same intent, `SCOPE` and seven questions, and runs the blast-radius proof in place. It sends the crewmate one combined review and writes one `## Review` section that jmerge's ready rule still accepts unchanged, with `Reviewers: 1`. jbus archives a review thread on the next pass after its PR merges or closes, and never archives one whose PR is open. Skills and docs that say "two reviewers" now say one. Tests cover each of these, and `make check` exits 0.

### Reviewers
- Reviewer A: 8 findings
- Reviewer B: 4 findings
- Both answered the seven questions. They overlapped on three points: how "closed" is decided, the stale Step 4 sentence, and the files outside `Where`.

### Act On

1. **"Closed" is inferred from a PR's absence, and that inference now drives a destructive archive** (A2, B1). `shut()` calls a slug closed when its Result URL is missing from the 100-item `world.open` list. Raw URL matching, a 101st open PR, or a URL that differs only in form would therefore archive the review thread of an open PR. That breaks the "never archived" Done when line, and jbus never undoes an archive. B1 adds that `watch.pull` already decides closed by a different rule, so the two views now disagree; the new `eta`/`pull/8` test is a case of this. The fix answers both reviewers:
   - Define "merged or closed" in one place.
   - Before archiving, confirm the state from GitHub (`gh pr view --json state`, cached like `merged.json`), so an absence alone never archives.
   - Reusing `watch.pull` alone isn't enough, because it is also absence-based.

2. **The jmerge "new shape" test never contains a listed finding** (A1). `Findings:` in the template has no `": "`, so the fill is skipped and the `- warning …` item is dropped. jmerge then sees `found == 0`, which means the rule "every listed finding has its `Finding:` line" is never exercised. That Done when test is the only proof that `ready.py` needs no change, so it has to hold a real finding. Add a negative case too: the same section without the `Finding:` line must not be ready.

3. **`docs/flow.html:214` still says "Two reviewers … then settles itself"** (A3). This directly misses the Done when line "any other skill or doc … says one". It is hand-written, and no test catches it. Fix the text. A `grep`-style check in `test_flow_doc.py` for "two reviewers" would also stop it coming back.

4. **Step 4 claims an independent check that no longer exists** (A6, B2). `skills/pr-review/SKILL.md:232` says to judge "against what the reading was not given: the brief's decisions". In one thread, the reading *was* given them. This skill text is the product of the change, and the sentence tells the reviewer it has a cross-check it lacks. Reword it to say what the judgment step adds now: re-checking each claim against the repo, and the dismissal discipline.

### Consider

- **`"archive"` as a mode key in a prefix-keyed map** (A4). Computing `ended` once in `settle` and deriving `("settle", "archive")` per thread from `slug_of` and the role removes the special case and the `shelve` propagation. It's a real simplification. The tradeoff is churn, but the Act On #1 rework touches `shut`/`settle` anyway, so it costs little to do it then.
- **A merged PR whose last Review is `not run` keeps its review threads** (A5). The Done when line doesn't condition archiving on the verdict. In practice jmerge won't merge such a PR, so the gap mostly hits the closed-unmerged case. Either archive the non-busy review threads of ended slugs regardless of verdict, or say in `docs/jbus.md` that they are kept on purpose.

### Intent
> Section 4 of the /deeper design: add a `Proves it:` line to `templates/brief.md`, right after `Done when:`. The brief parser and jbus's pre-launch checks, which sit beside `dispatch.designed`, accept the line only when it names something outside the agent: a test, a metric, a dataset, an external judge, or the user. They refuse an empty line, the template's own text, and any proof by the crew, crewmate, reviewer, agent, "self", "the model", or a review alone, each with a one-line reason. Briefs that have no line are refused or grandfathered without stranding an approved row. The change also needs tests for every kind, home-skill and `docs/` updates, and a green `make check` and `jgauge test-slot`.

### Reviewers
- Reviewer A: 7 findings
- Reviewer B: 6 findings
- Both reviewers found the same central flaw independently: the `_OUTSIDE`-first precedence combined with loose patterns. They also agreed on the duplicated head loop, the unused `Brief.proof`, the `<` heuristic and the two Done-when items that can't be verified from the diff. Both answered the review skill's questions.

### Act On

1. **Loose `_OUTSIDE` patterns let self-referential proofs through** (A1, B1, and B2 for the missing tests). `proof()` accepts a line on the first `_OUTSIDE` match and never consults `_SELF`. These lines all pass:
   - "make sure the reviewer is happy" is accepted as a test.
   - "self-test" is accepted, because `\btest\b` matches across the hyphen.
   - Any backticked text is accepted, for example `` `the crewmate` ``.
   - "the reviewer is 100% sure" is accepted as a metric.
   - "the model is the judge" is accepted as an external judge.
   - "the reviewer gives his word" is accepted as the user.

   Each of these maps to a phrase the Done-when line explicitly says must be refused. `_ready` launches whenever `proven()` returns `""`, so this check is the only gate. The fix is to make the outside patterns specific:
   - a test path or test name;
   - a command only when it starts with a known tool (`make <target>` but not "make sure", `uv`, `pytest`, `jbus`);
   - `%` only next to a metric word;
   - "his word/pick/eye" removed, or tied to "the user".

   Then add `REFUSED` cases that run `parse.proof` on every example above. The current tests only cover the happy side of the precedence rule, which is the riskiest part of the change.

2. **A missing `Proves it:` line is exempt forever, not only for briefs already queued** (A2). The Done-when line asks for queued briefs to be grandfathered. The code instead exempts any brief that lacks the line, including briefs written after this change. That leaves the requirement enforced by prose alone. `docs/jbus.md:85` claims a missing line means "written before the line was asked for", but nothing checks that claim. The fix is to tie the exemption to something the queue already records, such as the row's `approved` time or `brief_sha` before a cutoff, and gate everything later. This still meets "don't strand an approved row".

### Consider

- **A brief that fails both checks costs two gates and two re-approvals** (A3). Today `proven()` only runs when `designed()` passes. Every round costs the user an edit and an approval. The fix stays inside `dispatch.py`: collect both faults, send one gate keyed by sha, and drop the `short, kind` juggling. It is cheap and saves the user a round trip, but it is not a correctness issue.
- **Template-text detection by a leading `<`** (A6, B5). Stripping the brackets from the guide text lets it pass, and a real line such as `<= 50 ms p95` is wrongly refused. Comparing against the template's actual line, or matching `^<[^>]*>$`, is exact and cheap. "Refuses the template's own text" is a Done-when item, so this should be fixed if it is still possible after fix 1. Tightening the patterns may already stop the bracket-less guide text from matching.
- **`Brief.proof` and `Proof.said` have no consumer outside the tests** (A5, B4). This change added them, so leaving them unused is this change's leftover. Either remove them or show them on the jbriefs page.

### Noted

- **Duplicated head-line loop and a second check-specific branch in `_ready`** (A4, B3). A shared `head_line(text, label)` helper in `jbriefs.parse` would be the right shape. Moving `designed` there touches a rule that is marked do-not-touch, so that part is noted for later. The `_ready` branch goes away if A3's fault list is adopted.
- **Two Done-when items cannot be checked from the diff** (A7, B6). One is the grandfather-or-refuse statement in the Result; the other is one real queued brief run through the launch check with the line printed. Check both in the Result before merging. If Act On item 2 changes the grandfathering rule, the Result's statement has to change with it.

### Dismissed

None. Every finding was concrete and tied to changed lines. The nits are real, just small.

### Agreement Map

The two reviewers converged on almost everything. Both independently found the precedence/loose-pattern hole, and each added near-miss examples the other missed, which strengthens the case for it as the headline issue. They diverged in two places:
- **A alone** caught the permanent exemption (A2) and the double-gate cost (A3). Both concern how the check interacts with the queue and the user's approvals, not the parser itself.
- **B alone** framed the test gap as a separate finding (B2). It is folded into Act On 1.

The pattern suggests the parser logic was built against its own examples, without adversarial cases. The dispatch integration works, but it carries an exemption broader than the task asked for.

### Intent
> Section 3 of the /deeper design: a step in the home skill's brief writing, not a separate file. It runs on its own for research, perf, analysis and outcome briefs, with its own copy of the four questions. Answer 2 goes to the scout's `Read:` or the request's sources, answer 3 goes in the brief for the crew, and answer 4 goes in `Proves it:`. Mechanical fixes, docs changes and known-cause bug fixes skip it. `/deeper` stays manual. `templates/brief.md`, `skills/deeper/`, the principle and the parser are not touched.

### Reviewers
- Reviewer A: 6 findings
- Reviewer B: 7 findings
- The two did not agree on everything. Both answered the review skill's questions.

### Act On

**1. The step routes answers into an `Instruments:` line nothing defines, and a home-written `Read:` line that the template forbids.** (A1, B1)
- The step sends answer 3 to a brief's `Instruments:` line. That line exists nowhere in the template, the crew skill, the scout skill or the parser.
- The step also tells the home to write `Read:` on its own briefs. `templates/brief.md:17` tells it to leave that line out.
- The phrase "though the home wrote it" admits the clash but does not resolve it.
- Effect: a home that reads the template first, as it is told to, gets opposite instructions. A scout writing the brief from a request never learns about `Instruments:`, so answer 3 is lost.
- The template is under "Do not touch", so the fix has to happen in the step:
  - Put answer 3 in the brief for the crew using lines the template already has, such as a plain task-body sentence or the Done-when list.
  - Send answer 2 through the scout's `Read:`, which is what the Done-when line actually asks for.
  - Do not have the home write `Read:` itself.
- If the author still wants a dedicated field, record it in the Result as a follow-up for `templates/brief.md` and the scout skill.

**2. The case keys on the playbook name, not the kind of work.** (A2, A3, A4, B2, B3)
These five findings share one root cause and one fix. The kind of work is only consulted when the playbook is `none`, and three concrete failures follow:
- **`bug-fix` always skips.** But `playbooks/bug-fix.md` is the playbook for root-causing a defect, including one whose cause is unknown. The principle exempts only proven-cause fixes, and the test pins this mismatch as "known bug". This breaks the boundary in the second Done-when line.
- **Outcome work rarely gets the step.** Outcome work carried by `feature`, `autonomous-run`, `swarm` or `arena` skips it. The only route to the step is "no playbook", so the intent's "outcome briefs" is barely met.
- **A scout request is judged by the scout's playbook.** That is always `investigation` or `trace-forensics`, so every request runs the step, even one that briefs a refactor or docs change. Its answers 3 and 4 then get pushed onto that brief.

The hand-kept list of ten playbook names is a prose rule that will drift. The current test only checks one direction (listed names exist as files).

The fix: make the stated kind of work the block's input in every case (research | perf | analysis | outcome | known-cause-fix | mechanical | docs). For a request, use the kind of the task being briefed. The name list and its drift go away. The test then pins the kinds instead of file names.

  - Either way, one sentence in the step closes the gap.
- **The tests run the block but never check that the lines it names exist in the template.** (A6)
  - Once Act On 1 is fixed, a small test asserting that each named destination appears in `templates/brief.md` or `templates/scout-request.md` would have caught that finding.
  - It is cheap, though it is a text-matching test rather than an executing one.
- **"The block under it" points about 90 lines away, into another section.** (B5)
  - Name the section instead. It is trivial to fix, and the home is an agent following this text literally.

- **A prose-only extra skip ("Done when already names its data, instruments and judge").** (B6)
  - This is a real prose rule, but it is low impact. It can fold in as one more kind once Act On 2 lands.

  - The Result must show both outputs. It must also show how the "one brief after the merge" proof was checked beforehand, as the Proves-it line requires.

  - playbook-keyed classification, including the `bug-fix` mis-skip and the hard-coded list (A2, A4, B2, B3)

- "self-test"
- "`` `the crewmate` checks it``"
- "the reviewer is 100% sure"
- "the model is the judge"
- "the reviewer gives his word"
- "reviewed by the crewmate on github"

- "a test" needs a path (`tests?/\S+`, `test_\w+`) or a backticked command that starts with a known tool (`make`, `uv`, `pytest`, `jbus`).
- `make` counts only with a target, never in "make sure".
- `%` counts only near a metric word.
- "his word/pick/eye" goes, or is tied to "the user".
- "judge" counts only with an external qualifier.

### Reviewers

- Reviewer B: 4 findings

### Act On

**1. `shut()` infers "closed" from absence, and the result is a destructive archive.** (A2, B1)
`shut()` treats a slug as closed when its Result's `Branch:` URL is missing from `world.open`. Three things put a slug in that state while its PR is still open:
- The PR falls outside the `--limit 100` list.
- The URL differs only in form from GitHub's.
- The PR is keyed under another slug.

In each case the review thread of an open PR is settled and archived. That breaks the Done when line "a review thread of an open pull request is never archived", and jbus never undoes an archive.

B adds that `watch.pull()` already decides MERGED/CLOSED, and the two rules already disagree on the test's own `eta` case. The fix is to drop `shut()` and derive "ended" from `watch.pull()`, which returns `Pull.MERGED`/`Pull.CLOSED`. If that rule also infers from absence, confirm `CLOSED` from GitHub's real state before archiving. The test should include an open PR that is missing from the open list.

**2. The jmerge "new shape" test lists no finding, so it never exercises findings-answered.** (A1)
The template's `Findings:` line has no `": "`, so the filled value is never written. The section reaches `ready.py` with `found == 0`. The Done when line asks for a test that jmerge reads a new-shape section as ready, meaning findings listed and answered, and this test passes even if that matching breaks.
- Write the `- warning …` item under `Findings:` explicitly.
- Add the negative case: the same section with the `Finding:` line removed must not be ready.

**3. `docs/flow.html` still says "Two reviewers… then settles itself".** (A3)
This is a Done when line left unmet ("any other skill or doc… says one"). The page is hand-written, not generated, so the docs sweep won't fix it. The edit is cheap, and the Done when line authorizes touching the file even though it isn't on `Where`.

### Intent
> Add a `Proves it:` line to `templates/brief.md`, right after `Done when:`. The brief parser (`src/jbriefs/parse.py`) and jbus's pre-launch checks (beside `dispatch.designed`) accept it only when it names something outside the agent: a test, metric, dataset, external judge, or the user. It refuses empty lines, the template's own text, and proofs by the crew, crewmate, reviewer, agent, "self", "the model", or a review alone, with one line saying why. Briefs without the line are refused or grandfathered without stranding an approved row. The change is tested per kind, documented in the home skill and `docs/`, and `make check` passes.

### Reviewers
- Reviewer A: 7 findings
- Reviewer B: 6 findings

### Act On

**1. The `_OUTSIDE` patterns are loose and checked first, so self-referential lines pass the gate.** (A1, B1, B2)

Both reviewers independently traced concrete inputs that pass:
- "make sure the reviewer is happy"
- "self-test"
- ``the `reviewer` says so``
- "the reviewer is 100% sure"
- "the model is the judge"
- "the reviewer gives his word"

These lines are exactly what the task says to refuse. `_ready` launches whenever `proven()` returns `""`, so this regex set is the whole gate. As written, it rejects only lines that avoid every common word.

The precedence rule ("a test the crewmate runs is still a test") is right in spirit, but it needs the outside match to really be outside:
- a path or test name
- a backticked command with a known tool
- `make <target>`, but not "make sure"
- a `%` only near a metric word
- a judge that isn't the model

B2 is the test side of the same gap: `REFUSED` has no near-miss cases. Every example above should go into `REFUSED` and run through `parse.proof`.

**2. A missing `Proves it:` line is exempt forever, not only for briefs queued before the change.** (A2)

`proven()` returns `""` whenever the line is absent, for any brief. Leaving the line out is therefore a permanent way around the gate, and the requirement survives only as prose in the home skill. The Done-when line asked for a choice about *existing queued* briefs; this code exempts all future briefs as well.

The fix is to grandfather by something the queue already records, such as approval time or brief sha before a cut-off, and to gate on anything later. That keeps approved rows from being stranded, which is the constraint the task set, and it closes the bypass. It is a single-reviewer finding, but the execution path is concrete and it defeats the feature's purpose.

**Two failing checks produce two sequential gates and two re-approvals.** (A3, and the `_ready` half of B3)

A brief with no Design line and a bad proof costs the user an extra edit-and-approve round. Gathering both faults into one gate keyed by the brief sha is cheap and stays inside `dispatch.py`. It also removes the `short, kind` juggling.

The tradeoff is how often this happens. It requires a brief that fails both checks, which is mostly old briefs. Worth doing if `_ready` is being touched anyway for the Act On fixes.

**Template-text detection by a leading `<`.** (A6, B5)

Both directions are real:
- A guide line with the brackets stripped passes as "a test", because the guide text contains "test".
- A genuine `<= 50 ms p95` line is refused.

Comparing against the template's actual line, or `^<[^>]*>$`, is exact and cheap. It fits naturally alongside the Act On 1 tightening. It is low-frequency, so it is not blocking.

**`Brief.proof` (and `Proof.said`) have no consumer outside tests.** (A5, B4)

The reviewers converged on the most important problem, the loose `_OUTSIDE` precedence, with largely different example inputs. That independent consensus is the strongest signal in this review: the gate's core logic doesn't yet do what the task says.

### Intent
> Add a `Proves it:` line to `templates/brief.md`, right after `Done when:`. The brief parser and jbus's pre-launch checks (beside `dispatch.designed`) accept it only when it names something outside the agent: a test or command, a metric, a dataset, an external judge, or the user. They refuse an empty line, the template's own text, and any proof by the crew, crewmate, reviewer, agent, "self", "the model" or a review alone, with one line saying why. Briefs without the line are refused or grandfathered without stranding an approved row, and the Result says which. The change is tested per accepted and refused kind, and the home skill's brief section and `docs/` are updated.

### Reviewers
- Reviewer A: 7 findings
- Reviewer B: 6 findings
- The two agreed on the central defect, the remaining structure findings and both "can't see it in the diff" items. They differed on severity and on two points only one of them raised: the grandfathering scope (A) and the double gate (A).
- The review skill's questions were asked. Both reviewers answered against them.

### Act On

**1. `_OUTSIDE` is checked first and is loose enough to accept the agent's own word** (A1, B1, plus B2 for the tests)
- `proof()` returns success on the first `_OUTSIDE` match and never consults `_SELF` after that.
- The reviewers independently found that each of these lines passes:
  - "make sure the reviewer is happy" and "the crewmate will make sure it works"
  - "self-test"
  - any backticked text, such as `` `the crewmate` checks it `` or `` `self` ``
  - "the reviewer is 100% sure"
  - "the model is the judge"
  - "the reviewer gives his word"
  - "reviewed by the crewmate on github"
- These are concrete inputs a home would plausibly write, and `_ready` launches whenever `proven()` returns "". This gate is the whole feature, and right now it refuses only phrases that contain no common word.
- The fix:
  - Make the outside patterns specific:
    - test paths and names (`tests?/\S+`, `test_\w+`)
    - backticks only around a command or path from a known tool
    - `make <target>`, never "make sure"
    - `%` only near a metric word
    - "his word" only tied to the user
  - Alternatively, require that something outside still matches once the `_SELF` spans are removed.
- B2's point belongs to the same fix: every case listed above passes the current suite. Add a `REFUSED` case for each one, run through `parse.proof`.

**2. A missing `Proves it:` line passes forever, not just for briefs queued before the change** (A2)
- `proven()` returns "" whenever `proves_it` returns None. Nothing ties that exemption to when a row was approved.
- A brief written tomorrow without the line therefore launches with no gate. The requirement survives only as prose in the home skill.
- The Done-when asked for the choice that doesn't strand approved rows. It did not ask for an open bypass.
- The fix: grandfather on something the queue already records, such as the `approved` time before a cut-off or the set of `brief_sha` values at merge, and gate anything later. This is the one finding raised by a single reviewer that I'm promoting. The execution path is concrete, and it defeats the gate as fully as #1 does.

### Consider

**3. A design fault and a proof fault cost two gates and two re-approvals** (A3)
- `proven()` runs only when `designed()` passes. A brief that fails both makes the user fix and re-approve twice.
- Every approval costs the user a round, and collecting both faults into one gate is a few lines.
- This also removes the `short, kind` juggling in `_ready`.
- I'd take it, but it is a cost issue, not a correctness bug.

**4. The head-line scanning loop is duplicated, and `proven` is a pass-through** (A4, B3)
- `proves_it` repeats `designed`'s loop line for line, in another package.
- Within this PR's scope, the fix is to:
  - drop the `proven` wrapper, or have `proves_it` return a `Proof` with an empty `why`
  - make `_ready` iterate over `(kind, check)` pairs, which falls out of #3 anyway
- A shared `head_line` helper that also serves `designed` touches code this PR may not change. It is noted for later.

**5. Template detection by a leading `<` is wrong in both directions** (A6, B5)
- It falsely refuses a real metric line such as `<= 50 ms p95 from jgauge` (B5).
- It accepts the template's guide once the brackets are removed (A6). Fixing #1 shrinks this side.
- Matching `^<[^>]*>$`, or comparing against the template's actual line, is trivial and exact.

- **The Result's grandfather statement and the printed launch-check run against a real queued brief can't be verified from the diff** (A7, B6). Check the brief's Result. The code and `docs/jbus.md:85` do state grandfathering, but see #2 for what it actually grandfathers.

None. No finding was wrong or a pure preference.

  - Severities differed (Warning vs. critical). I side with critical: the check is the deliverable, and the hole is easy to fall into by accident.

### Intent
> Replace pr-review's two reviewer subagents (A/B) with one review thread. That thread reads the PR's diff itself, posts one combined review and one `## Review` section that jmerge's ready rule still accepts, and is archived by jbus once the PR merges or closes, never while it is open. Every skill or doc that says "two reviewers" should say one, the tests should cover the skill text, the archive and the jmerge read, and `make check` should pass.

- Reviewer B: 4 findings

**1. `shut()` infers "closed" from a PR being absent from a 100-item open list, and archives on that basis** (A2, B1)
`src/jbus/threads.py:164`. A slug counts as closed whenever its Result URL string is missing from `world.open`. That list is capped at `--limit 100` and compared by raw string. So the 101st open PR, or a URL in a different form, gets its review thread archived. That breaks the Done when line "a review thread of an open pull request is never archived". Archiving is also the one destructive action jbus never undoes.

- B found the string-match problem, and a disagreement with `watch.pull` that the new test itself shows (`eta` / `pull/8`).

- Archive only on confirmed state: `world.merged`, or a PR that GitHub reports as `CLOSED` (cached the way `merged.json` caches merges).
- Define "merged or closed" in one place rather than a second rule beside `watch.pull`.
- Caution: B's suggestion to reuse `pull()` as-is would inherit the same absence inference. Use it only if its CLOSED is confirmed state.

`tests/test_pr_review_skill.py:1512-1534`. The template line is a bare `Findings:`, so the `": "` split never fills it. The section jmerge reads therefore has `found == 0`, and the "every listed finding has its `Finding:` line" rule is never exercised. This is the Done when test for jmerge compatibility, and right now it would pass even if matching findings to answers broke.

Fix:
- Write the `Findings:` item explicitly into the section.
- Add the negative case: the same section with the `Finding:` line removed must not be ready.

**3. `docs/flow.html` still says "Two reviewers, one lead … then settles itself"** (A3)

### Intent
> Run the Proves it, Size, Playbook and required-field checks at `jbus queue add`, so an incomplete brief is refused before it reaches the user. Keep the launch's checks as a backstop. Bind an approval to a deterministic meaning fingerprint over the fields that carry scope and risk, so typo, formatting, reordering and Task-only edits keep the go, while any change to a Done-when line, path, number or value re-asks. Store the fingerprint, the full `brief_sha` and the basis in the approval record, and make them verifiable by another bot. Old full-text-sha approvals keep working. Document the method and its limits in the PR and `docs/jbus.md`, and have `make check` prove it.

### Reviewers
- Reviewer A: 9 findings
- Reviewer B: 8 findings
- They agreed independently on the three most serious findings: template text passing `_filled`, negation keeping the go, and the duplicated check lists. Each also raised findings the other did not.

### Act On

1. **`queue add` accepts unedited template text for Task, Done when, Pull request and Review** (A1, B1). `_filled` only catches values that start with `<`. The template's own lines start with `"` or `-`, or use `a | b`.
   - So a brief copied straight from `templates/brief.md` is queued and put to the user. That is the exact failure the task exists to stop, and it breaks a Done-when line.
   - The docs and the home skill claim the opposite.
   - Fix: strip quotes and list markers before the check, then reuse `_template()`. Add a test that runs `queue add` on the raw template and expects a fault for every required field.

2. **The home skill hides "its go does not hold"** (A2). The skill captures the output of `queue add` but prints it only when the command fails. After a scope change, the home sees a plain success, and the user is not asked again until a later launch gates the brief.
   - The task's whole point is that a scope change re-asks at the right moment.
   - The fix is small and sits inside Where (`skills/home/SKILL.md`): print `$said` when it contains the void line, and say that the home then puts the brief to the user again.

3. **A negation by contraction keeps the go** (A3, B2). Stripping the apostrophe turns `shouldn't` into `shouldnt`. That is within two edits of `should`, so "should fire" and "shouldn't fire" pair as the same line.
   - The two-edit rule comes from the task. Joining contractions was the author's choice, and it is what puts a negation inside the allowance.
   - Fix: turn `n't` into a separate `not` token, and add a test that `should` → `shouldn't` re-asks.
   - Leave the near-antonym pairs (`include`/`exclude`, `import`/`export`) and the sorting that loses direction as they are. They follow from the spec. Name them in the known-limit section of the docs and the PR, which the task requires and which currently lists only `must`/`may` and `files`/`fixes`.

4. **The add checks and the launch checks are two hand-kept lists** (A4, B3). `faults` repeats `CHECKS` and `ASKED` by hand. A check added at launch later would silently skip `queue add`, which brings back the bug this task fixes.
   - Only the Design case has a parity test.
   - Fix: keep one tuple of checks in `jbriefs.parse`. `faults` loops over it, and `dispatch` builds its checks from the same tuple, keeping only the grandfathering. The launch is then a backstop by construction.
   - This also removes the double `designed()` call (A7).

### Consider

- **`scope` is stored but never checked, and can disagree with `holds`** (A5). A bot that compares `scope` hashes, which is the use the docs suggest, would refuse a typo-fixed brief that jbus would launch. That undercuts the "another bot can check" line of Done when.
  - Cheapest fix: have the docs tell bots to trust `verify`'s `holds` rather than comparing `scope`.
  - Checking `scope == fingerprint(meaning)` in `approved_text` is one line. It protects against hand edits to `queue.json`, which the task's Do-not-touch already rules out.
  - A version field for the method is good insurance, but nothing changes the method yet.
- **`asks.py` decides what to print with `endswith` on message constants** (A6, B5). This is a rule kept in prose. Rewording either constant silently breaks the CLI output. Returning a flag or always printing the line is cheap. Weigh it against the size of the change.
- **The PR says the launch checks are unchanged, but the playbook check is now stricter** (A8). The change is intended, but rows approved with a non-crewmate playbook will now gate at launch. Add one sentence to the PR description.

### Noted
- A7: smaller redundancies: a discarded `_filled` result for Size, and `ROUTING` dropped twice. The `designed()` duplicate goes away with Act On #4.
- A9: re-prioritising an old, incomplete row now requires rewriting it, which voids its go. This is theoretical, since every row queued today has every field.
- B4: `approve` does not run `faults`. This only matters for incomplete rows queued before this change, and the launch backstop still catches them.
- B6: greedy pairing in `_pairs` can re-ask when a valid pairing exists. It errs toward asking, so it is safe. Only the docstring overstates it.

### Dismissed
- B7, `asks.py` outside Where: the queue verbs live in `asks.py`, not `cli.py`. The Where line named the CLI layer loosely, and this is where that work belongs.
- B8, the PR description could not be checked: Reviewer A read the PR body and found it states the method, with the limit gaps covered in Act On #3. The line is met apart from that.

### Agreement Map
The reviewers converged on the three structural problems: the template-text gap, contraction negation, and the duplicated check lists. Each did so independently, which is a strong signal; all three are in Act On.

A alone traced the change into the home skill and found the swallowed void line. That is the most consequential single-reviewer finding, because the re-ask path the task asks for silently fails. A also caught the stricter playbook check and the `scope`/`holds` mismatch.

B's extra findings were edge cases that err safe or concern old rows, plus scope bookkeeping.

The pattern: the core design (the fingerprint, the record, the verify command) is sound. The gaps are where the new check meets its edges: the template's actual text, the contraction rule, the home's handling of the output, and keeping the add and launch checks in step.

### Intent
> Add sections 1, 2, 5 and 6 of the /deeper design, built on Felix Rieseberg's "four types of ambition" (Depth):
> - a manual `skills/deeper/` skill that returns the four answers and a rewritten prompt, which a home gates through `jbus gate`;
> - a 25th principle, `depth-over-breadth`, which jdrift knows as a jstack source;
> - a `THIRD_PARTY.md` credit;
> - a blind, rerunnable eval in `evals/deeper/` whose committed Result says honestly whether /deeper won. A loss is a finding, not a reason to tune.

### Reviewers
- Reviewer A: 5 findings
- Reviewer B: 8 findings
- They overlap on two findings (raw has no control for the skill's list; `write()` wipes data before running). A1 and B1 approach the "outside" verdict from different angles and reach the same weakness. Neither reviewer reported a "Done when" line unmet outside the eval, so the principle count, jdrift, install and credit work appear sound.

### Act On

**1. The eval's "won" verdict rests on a measure that does not show an effect** (A1, B1)
- **A1:** A rescore of the committed run-2 briefs shows that the backtick branch of `OUTSIDE` (`evals/deeper/score.py`) produces the whole plain-to-deeper rise in "proof outside". Without it, the two arms are level (0.34 vs 0.33).
- **B1:** "Outside" flipped sign on 8 of 10 cases between run 1 and run 2. The only skill change between them was the output format (a fence became a block quote). The README states "won" on run 2 alone, against its own rule that only what both runs agree on counts.
- **Why it matters:** The task's central proof is an honest verdict, and it explicitly warns against re-running until the answer improves. The measure rewards code formatting, which the skill itself tells writers to use.
- **Fix:**
  - Count a backtick span only when it holds a command that is run, or drop the branch.
  - Rescore the committed briefs. This needs no model calls.
  - Rewrite the Result as "won on raw and instruments in both runs; proof outside not shown".
  - Drop the README's suggestion that `Proves it:` is "aimed at that gap" unless the corrected numbers support it.

**2. The "raw sources" claim is not backed** (A2, B2, consensus)
- Seven of the twelve `RAW` kinds match the skill's own question-2 list almost word for word.
- Instruments have a `beyond` count that excludes the skill's examples. Raw has none.
- Even so, `README.md` "What holds" says the result holds "not only by copying the skill's own examples".
- **Why it matters:** This is the second leg of the verdict. The fix is cheap: add a raw `beyond` and rescore the committed briefs, or narrow the sentence to instruments.

**3. The one rerun command deletes the committed results before doing any work** (A3, B3, consensus)
- `write()` in `evals/deeper/eval.py` runs `rmtree` on `runs/` and `deeper/` before 60 `claude -p` calls.
- If `claude` is missing, any call fails, or a call times out, the result is a partial `runs/`, mismatched `deeper/` files and a stale `key.json`. Nothing can resume.
- **Why it matters:** "Rerunnable by one command" is a "Done when" line, and this is the review's crash-halfway case.
- **Fix:** Write into a temporary directory and swap it in after `key.json` is written. Check `shutil.which("claude")` up front.

**4. Redaction fails open on a public repo** (B4)
- `_private` reads `~/.config` and ignores `XDG_CONFIG_HOME`, which `jleak.cli` honours.
- It also swallows `jleak.Missing` and returns no patterns.
- Cases, briefs and model output are then committed unredacted.
- **Why it matters:** Only one reviewer raised it, but it is a real leak path into a public repo. The silent fallback is the bug whatever the user's config location is.
- **Fix:** Resolve the path as `jleak.cli` does, and fail when the patterns cannot be loaded.

**5. The principle card claims playbooks that don't reference it** (B6)
- The card at `principles/depth-over-breadth.md:20` lists `perf-issue` and `investigation` as leaning on the principle. Neither playbook mentions it.
- The claim appears on `docs/jstack-explained.html`. On the other cards, the leans match real links.
- **Fix:** List only `deeper`. Linking the playbooks is outside the "Where" line and is for later.

**6. The gate's `Context:` placeholder invites lines that jbus drops** (B7)
- `skills/deeper/SKILL.md:67` reads "one line each", but `mirror.field` keeps only the `Context:` line. Answers 2 to 4 would be lost from the gate record.
- The test passes because it uses a single joined line, which the wording does not ask for.
- **Fix:** Change the placeholder to "on this one line, separated by semicolons".

### Consider

**`not_held` counts a phrase, and an outcome claim rests on it** (A4)
- "Seven of the ten had a Done when line their Result said did not hold" is read from a brief-wide count of "does not hold". That count misses "did not hold" and "doesn't hold" and includes text outside the Result.
- The outcome column is a "Done when" item, so its accuracy matters.
- **Tradeoff:** It is a secondary column. Limiting the search to the Result section and matching the tense variants is cheap, but relabelling the column as a phrase count would also be honest.

**`SELF` treats the bare word "review" as self-assessment** (B5)
- This penalises `rs-parallel-reviews` because of its subject, not because of who judges the result.
- **Tradeoff:** It distorts one case. It is worth folding into the `OUTSIDE` rework in Act on #1, since both edit the same measure, but it does not change the verdict by itself.

Every edit a home or a handoff makes to `$H/standing.md` is followed right away by `jbus snapshot`, so the edit is its own pushed commit in `~/.local/state/home`. - Reviewer A: 7 findings
- Reviewer B: 5 findings

**1. `take` has no lock, and snapshots now run at any time from many homes.** Raised by A1 and B1.
Before this change, only the timer ran `take`. Now every root and scoped home runs `add -A` → gitleaks → `reset`/`commit` → `push` against the same index, with nothing keeping the runs in step. Both reviewers trace the same concrete paths:
- **Lock collision.** Two runs collide on `.git/index.lock` and `_must` raises.
  - If the timer loses, `OnFailure` runs `--alarm` and pages the desk for a failure that isn't real.
  - If a home loses, its edit slides into someone else's commit, which breaks the "commit of its own" Done-when line.
- **Index reset mid-run.** A's `git reset -q` can land between B's `add` and `diff --cached`, so B prints "nothing changed".

This is a correctness issue on the exact guarantee the task asks for, and the fix is small and inside Where. Take a blocking `fcntl.flock` on a file under the tree's `.git` for the whole of add/commit/push, so concurrent runs wait instead of failing. Add a test that runs two snapshots concurrently, or at least holds the lock and shows the second run waits.

**2. The documented restore empties `standing.md` when `git show` fails.** Raised by A2 and B2.
The shell truncates the target before `git show` runs. It fails in ordinary cases:
- `<commit>` is the commit that created the file (the first rule ever),
- `<commit>` is the root commit,
- the hash is mistyped.

The doc's next step then snapshots the empty file, and the next start reads "no standing rules". This is a data-loss path in the one procedure this task exists to provide.

Keep the `git show` form the brief names, but write to a temp file and `mv` only on success: `... show <commit>^:<repo>/standing.md > <path>.tmp && mv <path>.tmp <path>`. Add one line on undoing the edit that created the file: there is nothing to restore, so remove the file and snapshot. Extend the test to cover undoing the creating commit.

**3. The handoff skill gains a duty to write standing rules.** Raised by A5 and B3.
"One it did not write yet goes there now" is a new behaviour that does not trace to the task. It also contradicts the sentence just before it ("the home wrote it to `standing.md` when it heard it"). In a skill prompt, a stray sentence like this changes what models actually do at every handoff.

The path-limited `log -p` / `show` undo still works, so the feature is not broken. Only the unscoped `git log` reads misleadingly.

The tradeoff: letting `--why` take the path(s) and commit only those (`git commit -- <path>`) gives clean commits. But it adds a positional argument and changes the call in three skill files, more than the brief's "one flag and one step". Homes (root and scoped) and the handoff skill run `jbus snapshot --why <text>` right after any edit to `$H/standing.md`, so each edit becomes its own pushed commit in `~/.local/state/home`. Tests that execute prove the commit and the restore, and `make check` exits 0.

### Reviewers
- Reviewer A: 7 findings
- Reviewer B: 5 findings

### Act On

**1. `take` has no lock, and snapshots now run at any time from many homes.** (A1, B1)
Before this change, one timer ran `take` twice a day. Now any home can run it whenever it edits `standing.md`.

Two failures follow from shared `.git/index.lock` and the shared index:
- If a home's snapshot overlaps the 08:30 or 17:30 run, one of them fails. If the timer's run loses, `OnFailure` fires `jbus snapshot --alarm` for a failure that isn't real.
- One run's `git reset -q` can unstage another run's `git add -A`. That run then prints "nothing changed", and the edit loses the commit of its own the task asked for.

Both reviewers named the same concrete execution path and the same fix: an exclusive `flock` on a file in `.git`, held across add, commit and push. It is inside `snapshot.py`, so it is in scope.

**2. The documented restore empties the live `standing.md` when `git show` fails.** (A2, B2)
The `> <repo>/standing.md` redirect truncates the file before `git show` runs. `git show` fails in ordinary cases:
- undoing the commit that created the file (rule 1), since its parent has no such path
- the root commit, which has no `^`
- a mistyped hash

The doc's next step then snapshots the empty file, and every home after that reads "no standing rules". This is the exact section the task asked for, so it has to be safe.

Fix:
- Document `git -C ~/.local/state/home restore --source=<commit>^ -- <repo>/standing.md`. It fails without touching the file.
- Say what to do when the bad edit created the file.
- Add a test for undoing the commit that created the file.

**3. Handoff gains a duty to write standing rules.** (A5, B3)
The new line "One it did not write yet goes there now, as one dated line" adds a place where rules get written. The task did not ask for it, and it contradicts the sentence just before it ("the home wrote it … when it heard it"). It changes what a home does at handoff, which is more than a nit.

Undo still works, because `log -p` and `show` are path-limited. What suffers is the plain `git log`: messages describe less than the commits contain. A related rare case is two homes editing the same `standing.md` before either snapshots, which puts both edits in one commit.

Added, removed or changed Done-when lines, paths, numbers and values re-ask. - Reviewer A: 9 findings
- Reviewer B: 8 findings
- Both readers answered the review skill's questions. They agreed on the four substantive findings and differed mainly on smaller items.

`_filled` (`src/jbriefs/parse.py:355`) only checks whether a value starts with `<`. So `"<the request…>"`, `- <a check>`, `open one when done | ask first` and `review | none` all pass.
- This breaks the Done-when line "refuses an incomplete brief", and the docs and home skill say the opposite of what the code does.
- The existing test misses it because it leaves out the template's quotes.

**2. A negated contraction keeps the go** (A3, B2)
Line 94 turns `shouldn't` into `shouldnt`, which is within two edits of `should`, so "should fire" and "shouldn't fire" fingerprint as the same in a Done-when line.
- The two-edit rule is the spec's. Joining contractions is the author's own choice, and it is what lets negation through.
- That defeats "still catching real changes to intent" in exactly the fields that carry scope.
- Fix: tokenise `n't` as `not`, and add a test that `should` → `shouldn't` re-asks.
- The cases that remain within the spec need adding to the stated limit in `docs/jbus.md` and the PR body: near antonyms (`include`/`exclude`, `import`/`export`) and swapped direction after fillers are dropped and words are sorted.

**3. The add checks and the launch checks are two hand-kept lists** (A4, B3)
`dispatch.CHECKS`/`ASKED` and `parse.faults` list the same checks separately, and only prose says they match.
- Keeping them in step is the point of this task. A check added later to the launch tuple would bring back "queued, approved, then gated" with no failing test.

The home skill (standing-rule writes and `skills/home/scoped-homes.md:7`) and the handoff skill run `jbus snapshot` right after any edit to `$H/standing.md`, so each edit is a commit of its own in `~/.local/state/home` and is pushed. The twice-daily timer stays. `jbus snapshot` takes `--why <text>`, which goes in the commit message. `docs/state.md` documents find → restore → re-snapshot. Executing tests cover the commit and the restore. `make check` exits 0. Where: `src/jbus/snapshot.py`, the three skill files, `docs/state.md`, `tests/test_jbus_snapshot.py`.

### Reviewers
- Reviewer A: 7 findings
- Reviewer B: 5 findings
- Both reviewers independently raised the same four issues: concurrency on the shared tree, the truncating restore command, the new handoff duty, and the out-of-Where doc file. They diverged only on nits. The review skill's questions were asked.

### Act On

**1. Snapshots now race each other and the timer on one git index, with no lock** (A1, B1)
Before this change, one timer ran `take` twice a day. Now any home, root or scoped, can run it at any moment against the same `~/.local/state/home`. There are two concrete failures:
- A collision on `.git/index.lock` makes `_must` raise. If the timer's run is the one that loses, `OnFailure` fires `jbus snapshot --alarm` and every project gets a false alert.
- One run's `git reset -q` (the gitleaks path) can land between another run's `add -A` and `diff --cached`. That run then prints "nothing changed", and the edit gets no commit of its own. This breaks a "Done when" line directly.

Both reviewers found this, with real execution paths. The fix is small and inside Where: hold an exclusive `flock` on a file in the tree's `.git` across add, commit and push in `take`, so concurrent runs wait instead of failing. Add a test that runs two `take`s concurrently against the temp tree.

**2. The documented restore command empties the live `standing.md` when `git show` fails** (A2, B2)
The `> <repo>/standing.md` redirect truncates the file before `git show` runs. The ordinary failure cases include a mistyped hash and, most likely of all, the commit that created the file: undoing a repo's first bad rule. In each, the user is left with an empty rules file, and the doc's next step tells them to snapshot it. The test passes only because its fixture's parent commit already has the file.

Fix in `docs/state.md`:
- Use a form that writes only on success: `git restore --source=<commit>^ -- <path>`, or `show … > tmp && mv`.
- Say plainly that when the bad commit created the file, the undo is to remove the file.
- Add a test for undoing the creating commit.

**3. The handoff skill gains a rule-writing duty nobody asked for** (A5, B3)
"One it did not write yet goes there now" is a new place where standing rules get written. It contradicts the sentence just before it ("the home wrote it … when it heard it"). The task asked handoff to snapshot after an edit, not to start making edits. This is a behavioural change to a skill that models follow. It is cheap to remove: keep only "after any edit to `$H/standing.md`, run `jbus snapshot --why …`".

### Consider

**4. A `--why` commit sweeps in the whole dirty tree, so its message mislabels it** (A3; B1's "mixed commits" point)
`git add -A` means the commit labelled "jstack standing rule 28 added" also carries queues, briefs, `merge.log` and other repos' changes from since the last snapshot.

The undo still works, because both `log -p -- <path>` and `show <commit>^:<path>` are path-limited. The damage is confined to the readability of an unfiltered `git log`, and to a looser reading of "a commit of its own".

A path-scoped `jbus snapshot --why … -- <repo>/standing.md` (`git commit -- <path>`) would make the message true and leave everything else for the timer. That is modest work inside `snapshot.py`.

The tradeoff: it adds a mode to `take`. It also does not cure B1's other sub-case, where two homes edit the same `standing.md` before either snapshots and both edits share one commit. Only the lock in Act On 1 narrows that window.

It is worth doing if you read the user's "a commit of its own" strictly. I lean towards doing it alongside the lock, since both live in the same function.

### Noted

A `jbus standing add` verb that writes the line and snapshots in one step is the durable fix, but it falls outside Where and is for later. Both also caught the invented handoff duty, though they disagreed on its severity. I side with A that it matters, because skill text is behaviour.

They split on framing the mixed-commit problem. A treated it separately, as a message-accuracy issue. B folded it into the concurrency finding. Separating the two clarifies the fix: the lock prevents failures and lost commits, and path-scoping makes the messages true.

The leftovers are minor and specific to one reviewer, which suggests that apart from the three Act On items the change is sound: the flag, the docs section and the executing tests do what the task asked.

It runs `jbus project add` through the same block new-home's step 3 uses, so the two cannot drift. A home that merges its own pull requests writes its id to `home-thread` before the add, so `jmerge` does not race it. A home that lets jbus merge leaves the file empty. jbus lists homes with a `home-id` and no project, but not parties or experts, in one quiet line, in `jbus status` and in the view's machine-row count. It adds nothing by itself. Docs and tests follow, and `make check` passes.

- Reviewer A: 6 findings
- Reviewer B: 5 findings
- Both found the same two issues independently: the stale-id wording (A1/B1) and the unreachable branches (A2/B4). The review skill's questions were asked. Neither reviewer reported an unmet "Done when" line or a file outside "Where".

### Act On

The change makes `home-thread` a deliberate write, but every later start of a self-merging home will tell the user that a stale id from before the `home-id` move is blocking merges. B traces the concrete harm: the user empties the file, and then both jbus and the home merge. That is exactly the race the task exists to prevent. Reword step 3's prose and the "not this home's id" clause in the state row, so an id written by "On the bus" reads as the switch set on purpose. Two independent reports and a real execution path make this the top item.
- **new-home step 4 still says this skill writes none of the four switches** (B2). `skills/new-home/SKILL.md:171,175`. The shared block now writes `home-thread`, so the same file holds two opposite rules. This is the same class of contradiction as A1/B1 and is inside "Where", so fix it here. The lines in `skills/handoff/SKILL.md:199`, `docs/state.md:18` and `docs/configuration.md:151` are outside "Where" and should be noted for a follow-up, not changed here.
- **`ME='<…, or nothing>'` invites a literal `nothing`, which would turn jbus merging off** (B3). `skills/new-home/SKILL.md:80-91`. The only check is that `<` and `>` are gone, and `merge.home_thread` only tests that the file is not empty. If a model fills in `nothing` or `none`, jmerge is silently disabled for the repo, and the line printed calls that a choice. This is a rule kept only in prose, with a cheap runtime fix: reject a value that is not shaped like a thread id and print `not filled in`. Step 5 runs the block only after step 4 printed `no project:`, so its `on the bus` and `jbus is not installed` branches are dead. The test reaches `on the bus` only by calling `machine.start()` outside the real trigger, so it proves a route a start never takes. The task's "leaves a present one alone" is actually done by step 4 not firing. A's remedy is the simpler one: drop the block and name the checkout from `git rev-parse --git-common-dir` in step 1 (or in step 4's `no project:` line). That removes a guarded block and a branch table, and the test should then exercise the step-4 → step-5 path. The tradeoff: this is not a correctness bug, but it is complexity plus a test that does not test the real flow, and it is cheap to remove.
- **The `status()` docstring says the opposite of the code** (A5). `src/jbus/cli.py:192-193`. `poll` writes the list into `status.json`, and both the view and `poll` read it back. A one-line fix that prevents a future misreading.
- **The new docs paragraphs split `jbus project add` from its argument bullets** (A6). `docs/jbus.md:190-192`. Move them below the list. This is trivial, and the bullets currently read as if they explain the wrong paragraph.
- **The `project` → `one` renames in `poll` and `alarm` are churn** (B5). `src/jbus/cli.py:459-461,532-542`. Only `status()` needs the rename. Either revert the other two, or also rename `first(project: …)` so the module is never shadowed. Low stakes, but these lines do not trace to the task.

### Intent
> The user said "there is no header or sidebars, navbars or helpers … in general the UI / UX feels subpar." The change should add:

> - a sidebar with "All" first, then each project with its waits count and a health dot, which becomes chips under 900 px
> - Room, jbus and Runners drawn once, as the machine's
>

### Reviewers
- Reviewer A: 8 findings
- Reviewer B: 9 findings
- Both answered the review skill's questions. They overlapped on six issues. The only "Done when" line either one found unmet is the header's last-read time (A3).

### Act On

1. **The header's "read" time shows the current time while the server is unreachable.** Raised by A3.
   - After `MISS` failed polls, `lost()` sets `NOW = Date.now()` and re-renders, so `page.html:752` shows "read \<now\>" and moves forward on every failure.
   - This breaks the "time of the last read" line in "Done when", in exactly the case where it matters.
   - Fix: keep the time of the last successful answer as its own value, set in `took`/`tookStack`, and show that.

2. **The sidebar health dot and the overview row chips use two different health rules, and they already disagree.** Raised by A2 and B5.
   - `troubles()` at `page.html:670` ignores `h.blind`. A project with only blind spots gets an amber chip on its row and a green dot in the sidebar.
   - It also prints "0 failed wakes, last error: X", a case the row chip already guards against.
   - Both reviewers found this independently, and the dot is a requested deliverable.
   - Fix: one helper per health fact, returning state, text and tip, which both the row and the dot read.

3. **The word caps were loosened by moving content out of what is counted, and the new `SHELL = 30` cap is fixed.** Raised by A4, B1 and B2.
   - `probe.js:104` now counts only `<main>`.
   - The machine row used to count toward the 250 and now counts toward neither cap. The header text no longer counts either.
   - This is a proxy check: the page did not get smaller, the measurement did.
   - `SHELL = 30` describes the three-project fixture (about 26 words today), not a design limit. Two more projects will fail it, contradicting the docstring.
   - Fix:
     - The machine row must count again.
     - Whether the nav chrome (project names in the sidebar) counts toward the user's caps is a question only the user can answer. Take the stricter default (count the whole first screen), pipe it to `jbus gate`, and carry on.
     - Any separate shell limit should scale with the project count and be tested with more than three projects.

4. **The sidebar stays empty for up to 15 s on a link to a project that does not exist.** Raised by A1.
   - This is a concrete ordering. The 404 arrives first, sets `S = null` and renders with no `STACK`. The stack then arrives, but its render sits behind `if (S)` (`page.html:1002`), so nothing redraws until the next poll.
   - Fix: drop the `S` guard (`put` already skips unchanged parts), and add a test that loads `#/nope` and checks the sidebar items on the first poll.

   - The stack request also fails silently (`function () {}`).
   - A false all-clear on a health dashboard is a correctness bug, not staleness.
   - Fix within this PR: show "unknown", not ok, when there is no stack read.

  - The header wraps, so at 900–1100 px with long crumbs the sidebar slides under it.
  - A shared CSS variable fixes it in one line. It is not covered by any "Done when" line, but it is a visible layout defect in the feature being added.
- **The theme control changed from a three-button group to a cycle button.** Raised by A8 and B9.
  - Nothing in the task asked for this, and it is untested.

The reviewers agreed on six issues: the word-cap loosening, the duplicated health rules, the file size, the sticky offset, the missing machine row on not-found, and the theme redesign. The consensus on the word caps and the health rules is the strongest signal in this review.
